deep.reconstruction:
Page 17 continues the previous page (conformal map of the ellipsoid of revolution onto a sphere, using the 'reduced' latitude psi and sphere radius r = a/sqrt(1-ee sin^2 P) at the standard parallel P). Here Gauss maps that sphere onto the plane by stereographic projection centred at the point (latitude P, central meridian), and works numerical examples. This is the 'conformal double projection' (spheroid -> sphere -> plane) later used for the Hannover survey and elsewhere.

1. Forward construction (as written). With plane coordinates x (along the central meridian, increasing southward: the north pole's image lies at x = -2r tan(45deg - P/2)) and y (increasing westward in the examples), define A, alpha and B, C by 2r tan(45-P/2) + x = A cos(alpha), y = A sin(alpha); 2r tan(45+P/2) - x = B cos(C), y = B sin(C). A and B are the distances of the point from the images of the north and south poles. The meridians are circles through the two pole images, the parallels are Apollonian circles (B/A = const). Gauss states: longitude difference lambda = alpha + C; latitude from tan(45 + psi/2) = B tan(45 - P/2)/A; convergence of meridians (inclination of the meridian to the abscissa line) = alpha - C; the meridian through the point is the line-like relation x + y tan((alpha-C)/2) = 2r tan((P-psi)/2) (a '2r' was struck out in the manuscript). I checked numerically that these are mutually consistent for the oblique stereographic projection (the latitude relation reproduces psi to machine precision).

2. Worked example 'Insel Planier'. Given x = +5628.56, y = +5679.67 (toises). log a (toises) = 6.5147609; adding log 1/sqrt(1-ee sin^2 P) = 0.0006588 (written 9.9993412) gives log r = 6.5154197; adding log 2 gives log 2r = 6.8164497. The ensuing columns compute alpha, C, then 45 + psi/2 = 66deg 35' 57.72'' (so psi = 43deg 11' 55.44''), phi = psi - small correction, and longitude: 6'53.258'' + 1'17.210'' = 8'10.468'' west of the central meridian 23deg 1' 54'' (Ferro), giving 22deg 53' 43.532''. My recomputation reproduces the 8'10.47'' exactly and psi = 43deg 11' 55.48''.

3. Earth constants. Quadrant factor: 1 + ee/4 + 7 e^4/64 + 15 e^6/256 with ee = 619/96100 (flattening 1/310): 10^7 x (1 + 0.0016103 + 4.5379e-6 + 1.57e-8) = 10016148.551; divided by pi/2 this gives a = 6,376,478 m (log a = 6.8045809), i.e. a is derived from a meridian quadrant of 10^7 metres (the original metre definition) via the inverse series of the meridian-arc expansion. In toises log a = 6.5147609 (1 toise = 1.949036 m).

4. Inverse problem (given phi, lambda find x,y): x + iy = 2r [cos(l/2) sin((P-psi)/2) - i sin(l/2) cos((P+psi)/2)] / [cos(l/2) cos((P-psi)/2) + i sin(l/2) sin((P+psi)/2)]. This is the oblique stereographic formula in complex form; for lambda = 0 it reduces to x = 2r tan((P-psi)/2), matching the meridian relation above. Numerical example with P = Goettingen (51deg 31' 55''), lambda measured from Goettingen: Brocken (phi 51deg 48' 12'', psi = 51deg 48' 9.57'') gives x = -30411, y = -47427 (page; I get -30411.1, -47425.6), distance 56339 and convergence = twice the argument of the denominator = 32'22'' (I get 32.37' = 32'22''). The unit mark on the page (triple-prime) is unclear; the magnitudes match metres. Similar calculations for Seeberg (phi 50deg 56' 8'', psi 50deg 56' 13.41'', lambda 47'30'') and Muehlhausen (51deg 12' 59'', psi 51deg 13' 1.85'', lambda 32'45'') give x = 66036, y = -55631, Delta = 86346 and x = 34957, y = -38125, Delta = 51725; my values agree to about 1 unit. The note 'aus den geod. Messungen in 1803 ungef.' with +35305, -35481 compares with older rough survey values; what exactly is compared is unclear.

5. Direction (arc-to-chord) correction. 'Endlich findet sich die Correction des Azimuths ... tang Corr = (x'y - xy')/(4rr + xx' + yy') genau.' The angle at point (x,y) between the straight plane line to (x',y') and the image of the great-circle arc. Derivation (mine): the image of a great circle is a circle through z, z' and the image of the antipode of z, w = -4r^2/conj(z); by the tangent-chord theorem the angle is arg((z'-w)/(z-w)) = arg(4r^2 + z' conj(z)), whose tangent is (xy' - x'y)/(4rr + xx' + yy') (up to Gauss's sign convention). The right-hand expression with 2r delta / (Delta/2) is an unclear alternative form, marked [?] in the transcription.

6. Series for the Goettingen region. Latitude phi = P + d, psi = phi + (1) d + (2) d^2 with log(1) = 7.39836-10 (about -0.0025 as coefficient: matches -ee cos^2P/(1-ee sin^2P)) and log(2) = 1.86733-10 (per second of arc squared, about 7.4e-9). Below it a table of the correction psi - phi in seconds for phi = 51, 52, 53, 54 deg (+4.80, -4.21, -13.03, -21.67; differences 9.01, 8.82, 8.64) and a 10-minute interpolation table, plus a table of (e/2) log10((1+e sin phi)/(1-e sin phi)) for phi = 49..54 deg (0.0021138, ...456, ...768, 0.0022073, ...372, ...663), which I verified to 7 places. These tables serve to get psi from phi quickly.
errors: Second-order coefficient (2): the series psi = phi + (1)d + (2)d^2 coefficient used here (and in the previous-page formulas psi = P + (1-ee)/(1-ee sin^2 P) d + ee(1-ee) sin2P/(4(1-ee sin^2P)^2) d^2, and the inverse with -ee sin2P (1-ee sin^2 P)/(4(1-ee)^2) e^2) is too small by a factor of 3. Differentiating the defining relation gives psi'' = 3 ee (1-ee) sinP cosP/(1-ee sin^2 P)^2 at phi = psi = P, so the true d^2 coefficient is 3 ee (1-ee) sin2P/(4 (1-ee sin^2P)^2) (and similarly the inverse has a factor 3). The page's log(2) = 1.86733 (7.4e-9 per arcsec^2) follows the 1/3-size coefficient (the correct value would be about 2.3e-8, log about 2.36).

Consequently the correction table psi - phi for P = Goettingen is inaccurate away from P: exact values (computed from the exact conformal-latitude relation) are +4.88, -4.15, -12.59, -20.44 arcsec for phi = 51, 52, 53, 54 deg versus the page's +4.80, -4.21, -13.03, -21.67; error about 0.06 arcsec at 52 deg, 0.4 at 53 deg, 1.2 at 54 deg (partly a neglected cubic term, mainly the factor 3).

Planier example: the final psi is written 43deg 11' 56.45'' (digits overwritten in the manuscript), but the doubled angle 66deg 35' 57.72'' above it gives psi = 43deg 11' 55.44'', agreeing with my recomputation 55.48''. The written 56.45'' looks like a one-second slip. The accompanying phi = 54.34'' is then only about 1.1'' below psi, whereas theory gives about 1.22'' (my phi = 54.26''); a small (about 0.1'') discrepancy, uncertain.
Minor: Brocken y = -47427 versus my -47425.6 (about 1.4 units); Seeberg psi 13.41'' versus my 13.48'' (consistent with the truncated series); not significant.

The sign conventions (y positive westward, x southward, lambda = alpha + C taken with matching sign) are implicit and not stated; for Seeberg and Muehlhausen lambda is written as east (+) while y is negative.

results.what: Stereographic projection of the sphere centred at latitude P, with pole-image distances A, B and angles alpha, C; longitude = alpha + C, latitude from tan(45+psi/2) = B tan(45-P/2)/A, meridian convergence = alpha - C
results.modern_name: Oblique (polar-angle/Apollonian-circle form of the) stereographic projection
results.usually_credited_to: Hipparchus/Ptolemy (stereographic projection); Gauss for the double projection use

results.what: Complex-form forward formula x+iy = 2r [cos(l/2) sin((P-psi)/2) - i sin(l/2) cos((P+psi)/2)] / [cos(l/2) cos((P-psi)/2) + i sin(l/2) sin((P+psi)/2)]
results.modern_name: Closed-form oblique stereographic projection in complex form (Mobius type)
results.usually_credited_to: Classical; compact complex form associated with Gauss/Schreiber for the Hannover and Dutch systems

results.what: Conformal double projection: ellipsoid -> sphere (conformal, equal scale at parallel P, radius a/sqrt(1-ee sin^2 P)) -> plane by stereographic projection, with numerical worked examples (Planier, Brocken, Seeberg, Muehlhausen)
results.modern_name: Gauss conformal double projection (Gaussian sphere + stereographic), basis of Hannover / Rijksdriehoek / Stereo-type systems
results.usually_credited_to: Gauss (Hannover survey, c. 1820s), Schreiber 1866 for the theory

results.what: Exact chord-to-geodesic direction correction tan(Corr) = (x'y - xy')/(4rr + xx' + yy') for the stereographic plane
results.modern_name: Arc-to-chord (direction reduction, 'Richtungsreduktion') correction, exact form for the stereographic projection

results.what: Earth semi-axis from a 10^7 m meridian quadrant using the inverse series 1 + ee/4 + 7e^4/64 + 15e^6/256 and flattening 1/310 (a = 6,376,478 m)
Series psi = phi + (1) d + (2) d^2 and interpolation tables of the correction psi - phi near Goettingen; second-order coefficient too small by factor 3
results.modern_name: Series expansion of the conformal (isometric-based) latitude

deep.surprise_reason: The page is applied geodesy: oblique stereographic projection, the spheroid-to-sphere conformal map (Gauss's double projection) and worked numerical examples. All of it is standard and Gauss's authorship of this projection scheme is already known (the published Nachlass and Schreiber's theory of the Hannover method). The only slightly notable features are the early date, the exact arc-to-chord direction formula and the Goettingen/Brocken/Seeberg/Muehlhausen numerical comparison with the 1803 measurements, plus a factor-3 slip in the second-order coefficient that I verified.
